artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Particle size, concentration, pressure, temperature, and catalysts increase reaction rate by increasing effective-collision frequency or by increasing the fraction of collisions with enough energy.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Every rate factor should be traced back to effective collisions: either collisions happen more often, or a larger fraction of collisions has sufficient energy.

steps.name: Start with collisions
steps.beat: A reaction speeds up only when effective collisions become more frequent.

steps.name: Change contact chances
steps.beat: Smaller particles, higher concentration, and higher pressure make successful contact more likely by increasing exposed surface area or particles per unit volume.

steps.name: Change particle energy
steps.beat: Higher temperature makes particles move faster and increases the fraction with energy greater than or equal to activation energy.

steps.name: Lower the barrier
steps.beat: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more particles have sufficient energy to react.

steps.name: Compare outcomes
steps.beat: Each factor raises rate through one or both collision levers: collision frequency and enough-energy fraction.

key_symbols.meaning: The rate-linked output that increases when collisions are more often successful.
The factor that changes exposed surface area.
The factor that changes number of particles in the same volume.
The factor that changes gas particle density by changing volume.
The factor that changes particle speed and enough-energy fraction.
The energy threshold lowered by a catalyst.
Collisions that fail because they lack sufficient energy or the right orientation.

interactivity_hooks: Particle size / surface area control: slide from large pieces to small pieces and watch exposed surface area and effective-collision frequency change.
Concentration control: increase particles in the same volume and watch collision frequency and initial rate rise.
Pressure control: compress gaseous reactants into a smaller volume and watch particles per unit volume and collision frequency rise.
Temperature control: raise temperature and watch particle speed plus the fraction above activation energy increase.
Catalyst / activation energy control: toggle catalyst on to lower the activation energy barrier and increase the fraction of particles with enough energy.
Compare mode: turn factors on one at a time to classify whether each mainly changes collision frequency, enough-energy fraction, or both.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: As reactants are used up, gas is produced more slowly, so the volume-time graph gradient becomes gentler and finally reaches zero when no more gas is formed.
artifacts.transferable_principle: On a product-time graph, the gradient at a point represents reaction rate, and a zero gradient means the reaction has stopped.

steps.name: Fast start
steps.beat: Many reactant particles are available, so effective collisions are frequent and gas volume rises steeply.

steps.name: Reactants fall
steps.beat: As reactants are consumed, fewer effective collisions happen per unit time and gas is produced more slowly.

steps.name: Gentler gradient
steps.beat: The graph still rises, but the gradient becomes gentler because each time interval adds less gas.

steps.name: Reaction complete
steps.beat: When no more gas is produced, the graph becomes horizontal and the reaction rate is zero.

key_symbols.meaning: The starting particles being used up during the reaction.
The product measured as volume of gas collected.
The graph that records accumulated gas volume over time.
The local slope that represents rate of reaction.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle between early, middle, and final time points to compare the graph gradient.
Drag a time marker along the curve to see the corresponding gas production rate.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Hydrogen gas escapes from the flask as the reaction proceeds, so the measured mass decreases quickly at first, then more slowly, and finally stops changing when the reaction is complete.
artifacts.transferable_principle: When a gaseous product escapes, the rate of mass decrease shows the reaction rate and the gradient becomes zero at completion.

steps.name: Gas escapes
steps.beat: The reaction produces hydrogen gas, and the gas leaves the flask instead of staying on the balance.

steps.name: Mass drops fast
steps.beat: At the start, effective collisions are frequent, so gas escapes rapidly and the mass-time graph is steep.

steps.name: Mass drops slower
steps.beat: As reactants are used up, fewer effective collisions occur and the graph becomes gentler.

steps.name: Mass levels off
steps.beat: When the reaction is complete, no more gas escapes and the measured mass stops decreasing.

key_symbols.meaning: The experimental setup whose mass is being measured.
The product leaving the setup and reducing measured mass.
The particles being consumed as the reaction proceeds.
The graph showing total mass decreasing over time.
The slope that shows how quickly mass is changing.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle whether gas is trapped or allowed to escape to see why the mass change depends on gas leaving.
Click graph regions to compare steep, gentle, and zero gradients.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Reactant particles form products only when they collide with both sufficient energy and the right orientation; missing either condition makes the collision ineffective.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Reaction rate depends on the frequency of effective collisions, not just the number of collisions.

steps.name: Collision happens
steps.beat: Two reactant particles meet, but a collision alone is not enough to form products.

steps.name: Energy checked
steps.beat: If the particles do not have sufficient energy, the collision is ineffective and no product forms.

steps.name: Orientation checked
steps.beat: If the particles meet in the wrong orientation, the collision is also ineffective even if they collide.

steps.name: Product forms
steps.beat: Only a collision with sufficient energy and the right orientation becomes an effective collision.

key_symbols.meaning: One reacting particle that must collide effectively.
The other reacting particle in the collision.
The minimum energy needed for the collision to be successful.
The product formed after an effective collision.

interactivity_hooks: Switch collision energy between low and sufficient to see whether product forms.
Rotate one particle to test right and wrong orientations.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Smaller reactant particles expose a greater total surface area, allowing more contact between reactants and increasing the frequency of effective collisions.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Increasing exposed surface area increases reaction rate when collisions occur at the surface.

steps.name: Large pieces
steps.beat: A few large reactant pieces expose only their outside surfaces to the other reactant.

steps.name: Smaller pieces
steps.beat: Breaking the same reactant into smaller pieces exposes more total surface area.

steps.name: More contact
steps.beat: With more exposed surface, more reacting particles can collide with the solid at the same time.

steps.name: Faster reaction
steps.beat: The frequency of effective collisions is higher, so the rate of reaction increases.

key_symbols.meaning: The lower-surface-area case.
The higher-surface-area case after particle size is reduced.
The contact area available for collisions.
Successful collisions occurring at exposed surfaces.

interactivity_hooks: Drag a particle-size slider from large pieces to smaller pieces and compare exposed surface area.
Toggle collision markers to compare effective-collision frequency in the two cases.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: A higher concentration places more reacting particles in the same volume, so collisions and effective collisions occur more frequently and the initial graph gradient is steeper.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Concentration changes reaction rate through particle number per unit volume; final product amount stays the same if the limiting reagent amount is unchanged.

steps.name: Same volume
steps.beat: Two containers have the same volume but different numbers of reacting particles.

steps.name: More particles
steps.beat: The higher-concentration container has more particles per unit volume.

steps.name: More collisions
steps.beat: Because particles are more crowded, collisions happen more frequently.

steps.name: Steeper start
steps.beat: The higher-concentration reaction has a steeper initial product-time gradient.

steps.name: Same final volume
steps.beat: If the limiting reagent amount is the same, the final volume of carbon dioxide produced is the same.

key_symbols.meaning: The slower comparison case with fewer particles per unit volume.
The faster case with more particles in the same volume.
The frequency of particle collisions.
The graph comparing reaction rates and final gas volumes.
The same final product amount when the limiting reagent is unchanged.

interactivity_hooks: Adjust concentration and observe particle density, collision frequency, and initial gradient together.
Toggle limiting reagent amount to see when final gas volume does or does not change.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Increasing pressure decreases the volume occupied by gaseous reactants, bringing particles closer together so there are more particles per unit volume and more frequent effective collisions.
artifacts.transferable_principle: For gaseous reactants, pressure affects rate by changing particle density and collision frequency.

steps.name: Lower pressure
steps.beat: Gas particles are spread through a larger volume, so collisions are less frequent.

steps.name: Volume decreases
steps.beat: Increasing pressure compresses the gas into a smaller volume.

steps.name: Particles closer
steps.beat: The same particles are now closer together, giving more reactants per unit volume.

steps.name: Faster reaction
steps.beat: More collisions occur between reactants, increasing the frequency of effective collisions.

key_symbols.meaning: The pressure change that compresses the gas.
The reacting particles whose spacing changes with pressure.
The compressed space that increases particles per unit volume.
Successful collisions occurring more often at higher pressure.

interactivity_hooks: Drag the piston to change volume and observe particle density.
Compare collision counts at low and high pressure over the same time interval.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Increasing temperature raises average kinetic energy, making particles move faster and increasing the fraction with energy at or above activation energy, so effective collisions become more frequent.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Temperature increases reaction rate by changing both collision frequency and the proportion of collisions energetic enough to react.

steps.name: Lower temperature
steps.beat: Particles move more slowly and fewer have enough energy to overcome activation energy.

steps.name: Temperature rises
steps.beat: The average kinetic energy of the particles increases.

steps.name: Faster motion
steps.beat: Particles move faster, so collisions happen more often.

steps.name: More above threshold
steps.beat: A larger fraction of particles has energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.

steps.name: Higher rate
steps.beat: Both effects increase the frequency of effective collisions and raise the reaction rate.

key_symbols.meaning: The lower-temperature case with less kinetic energy.
The temperature increase that raises average kinetic energy.
The threshold energy needed for reaction.
Particles with enough energy for effective collisions.

interactivity_hooks: Move a temperature slider to change particle speed and above-threshold fraction.
Toggle between motion view and energy-distribution view to connect the two explanations.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, so more reacting particles have sufficient kinetic energy to overcome the barrier and collide effectively.
artifacts.transferable_principle: A catalyst changes rate by lowering the activation energy barrier without changing the reaction yield or being chemically altered.

steps.name: Uncatalysed path
steps.beat: Without a catalyst, particles must overcome a higher activation energy barrier.

steps.name: Catalyst added
steps.beat: The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway.

steps.name: Lower barrier
steps.beat: The alternative pathway has a lower activation energy requirement.

steps.name: More effective collisions
steps.beat: More reacting particles now have enough kinetic energy to react successfully.

steps.name: Catalyst unchanged
steps.beat: The catalyst changes the rate of reaction without being chemically altered or changing the yield.

key_symbols.meaning: The higher activation energy requirement.
The substance providing an alternative pathway.
The reduced energy barrier in the catalysed reaction.
Particles that now have sufficient energy to react.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle catalyst on and off to compare activation energy barriers.
Adjust particle energy and see whether each particle clears the uncatalysed or catalysed barrier.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: When magnesium mass and excess acid conditions keep the final hydrogen amount unchanged, increasing acid concentration makes the initial gradient steeper while the final gas volume remains the same.
artifacts.transferable_principle: For rate graph questions, separate rate clues from amount clues: concentration changes the initial gradient, while the limiting reagent controls the final plateau.

steps.name: Identify the change
steps.beat: The acid concentration increases from 1.0 mol/dm3 to 2.0 mol/dm3 under otherwise same conditions.

steps.name: Predict the rate
steps.beat: Higher concentration gives more particles per unit volume, so the reaction starts faster.

steps.name: Check final amount
steps.beat: The magnesium mass is still 0.5 g and the acid is in excess, so the final hydrogen volume stays the same.

steps.name: Choose the curve
steps.beat: The correct curve is the one with a steeper initial gradient but the same final plateau as graph 1.

key_symbols.meaning: The original reaction curve for 1.0 mol/dm3 acid.
The curve showing the faster reaction at higher concentration.
The unchanged final hydrogen volume.
Options that change the final amount despite the same magnesium amount.
The curve matching both the rate and amount clues.

interactivity_hooks: Click each candidate curve to test it against the two checks: initial gradient and final plateau.
Toggle clue labels for concentration, excess acid, and magnesium mass.
